name: Diego Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Diego. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say is confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do office fit-outs for Northgate Construction, the big contractor, on a fourteen-storey tower by the ring road. Metal stud walls, plasterboard, doors, ceilings, the inside of the building once the frame's up. Since spring we've had a layout robot on our floors, a little machine about the size of a vacuum cleaner that drives around and prints the wall lines on the concrete from the drawings. I'm the one who sets it going each morning, because nobody else wanted to.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up being the robot person?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Curiosity, mostly. I use the AI on my phone every day, to check drawings, to ask why the fire stopping detail says one thing and the spec says another, to write my messages to the site manager without swearing. When the robot turned up I read the manual on my lunch break and the supplier's man, Ollie, showed me the rest. My wife Paula says I've always been like this, I bought one of the first video recorders on our street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Bit of a let-down, but all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you it was useful but not magic, which is what I've always said. The layout robot saves us maybe two days a floor, that's real, but it doesn't hang a door. I might post a video of it in the trade forum, people like watching it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it changes nothing much for me. I'd keep enjoying the gadgets and keep hanging plasterboard. My body's the clock that matters, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same job at Northgate, same tools, and I'd keep using the AI for the small stuff. I'd keep putting money aside, we've got about five months of bills saved. Retire at sixty-five or so and get a better drone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robot saves two days a floor. What did the crew think of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At first they called it R2-D2 and tried to trip it up with offcuts. Now they wait for it like a tea trolley, because once the lines are down, everyone knows exactly where to build. Nobody lost a job over it, it just took away the bit where we argue about measurements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you less bored in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A machine that lifts the plasterboard sheets onto the ceiling. They exist, sort of. If my back lasts till sixty-five because of something like that, I'd count that as AI doing its job.

S0.say: I always said it was useful but not magic. The layout robot saves us maybe two days a floor, which is real, but it doesn't hang a door.
S0.think: It changes nothing much for me, I'd keep enjoying the gadgets and hanging plasterboard. My body's the clock that matters, not AI.
S0.do: Stays at Northgate with the same tools and keeps using AI for small tasks. Keeps saving towards about five months of bills and plans to retire around sixty-five.
S0.quote: At first they called it R2-D2 and tried to trip it up with offcuts. Now they wait for it like a tea trolley
S0.fieldNote: He already runs a site robot and enjoys it, so a plateau mildly disappoints him. He frames AI's best use as saving older bodies from strain. Good-humoured and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strong change, time to adjust. That's roughly what I see starting on my site already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, learn it or get left behind, but say it kindly. I'd tell the younger ones to get on the machines early. And I'd say firms and the government both have to help people over the bump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do fine. I'm already the guy who runs the robot. If they bring in more machines, someone has to set them up, check them, fix them when they get stuck on a cable, and I'd want that to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Northgate to make me the site's machine lead, with a bit more pay, and I'd take any course the supplier offers. I'd read up on the plasterboard-lifting robots and the drilling ones. And I'd put any extra pay straight into savings, so I can retire on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. It's like a new toy at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stan, who's sixty-two and won't go near the layout robot. He's a better carpenter than me, honestly, but he thinks the robot's watching him. I'd want to be the one who shows him, not the one who replaces him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said firms and government both have to help. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Firms pay for the training, because they get the savings. The government makes sure older people can retire a bit early if their job really goes. Not handouts for everyone, just a sensible bridge.

S1.say: Learn it or get left behind, but I'd say that kindly. Firms and the government both have to help people over the bump.
S1.think: I think I'd do fine, because I'm already the one who runs the robot. Someone has to set up, check and fix new machines, and I want that to be me.
S1.do: Asks Northgate to make him site machine lead with a pay rise and takes the supplier's courses. Reads up on plasterboard-lifting and drilling robots and saves any extra pay.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like getting a new toy at work.
S1.quote: I'd want to be the one who shows him, not the one who replaces him.
S1.fieldNote: He sees a clear role for himself as the machine lead and is already halfway there. His centrist view comes through as a practical split of responsibilities between firms and government. He thinks of an older colleague with real respect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. Full AGI and robots doing hands-on work. Okay, that's a big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say, this is coming fast, so let's be sensible and not panic. We'd need the government to do something quick for people losing work. I'd say it calmly, because panicking never fixed anything on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be one of the last on site to go. Even with AGI, someone has to get the robots off the lorry, set them up on a wet floor with cables everywhere, and sort it when one drives into a stairwell. I'd be sixty, I'd probably have two or three years of that, and then retire a bit early with what we've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to Ollie at the robot supplier and ask if they need site technicians, because they'd be swamped. I'd learn everything they'd teach me, using the AI to study at night. And I'd stop any big spending and push savings up from five months to as much as I could, ready for an early exit around sixty-two or sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, more like before a big pour, when you know you've got to get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound fairly relaxed for the fastest picture. Is that really how you'd feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. I'd worry a bit for Paula, she's on reception at a school and an AI could answer phones, I know that. But I've already been working next to a robot for six months, and it still needs me every morning. That makes me think the first couple of years would need people like me more, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years of warning, what would you do in the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ring Ollie, honestly. And sit down with Paula and work out what we'd need if I stopped at sixty-two instead of sixty-five. Then I'd go back to work and keep doing what I'm doing, because that's what makes me useful.

S2.say: This is coming fast, so let's be sensible and not panic. The government would need to move quickly for people losing work, and I'd say that calmly.
S2.think: I think I'd be one of the last on site to go, because someone has to unload, set up and rescue the robots on a messy floor. I'd get two or three years of that, then retire a bit early.
S2.do: Asks his contact at the robot supplier about becoming a site technician and studies everything they teach, using AI at night. Stops big spending and builds savings for an early exit around sixty-two or sixty-three.
S2.feel: Uneasy rather than scared, like before a big concrete pour.
S2.quote: I've already been working next to a robot for six months, and it still needs me every morning.
S2.fieldNote: His daily work with a site robot makes him believe the transition will need people like him. I gently tested his calm and he acknowledged a worry about his wife's job. His exit plan is concrete: stop at sixty-two or sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031. I'd be sixty-three. That suits me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get this right, so firms should train people now. I'd tell the young lads to get on the machines early. And I'd say the government should plan for older workers, not wait for a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one's close to perfect for me. Five years running robots on site, then retiring around sixty-three or sixty-four, right when the work runs out. I'd be the bridge between the old way and the new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Northgate to make me machine lead, and do a proper certificate in site robotics at the college. I'd keep saving and probably pay off the car. And I'd train others, Stan included if he'd let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Even a bit pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Pleased? Even though the end point is the same as the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The end point's the same, but the timing's different. In two years I'm rushing to keep up. In five, I'm ahead, I get to use what I've learned, and I leave when I'm ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your kids anything different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mateo's a paramedic, I'd tell him he's probably fine, people want a human when they're hurt. Ines runs a little café. I'd tell her to think about what makes people come to her instead of a machine, the chat, the regulars.

S3.say: There's time to get this right, so firms should train people now and young lads should get on the machines early. The government should plan for older workers instead of waiting for a crisis.
S3.think: This one's close to perfect for me: five years running robots on site, then retiring around sixty-three or sixty-four. I'd be the bridge between the old way and the new.
S3.do: Presses Northgate to make him machine lead and takes a college certificate in site robotics. Keeps saving, pays off the car and trains colleagues, including the older one who avoids the robot.
S3.feel: Calm and even a bit pleased.
S3.quote: I'd be the bridge between the old way and the new.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, the timing fits his retirement almost perfectly, and he says so. He would invest in a formal certificate and in training others. His advice to his children is practical and specific.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. I'd be sixty-eight. Probably flying drones over the reservoir.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, ten years is a gift, use it. Firms, government, people, everyone's got time to prepare. I'd say that to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it barely touches me. I'd ride the early machines at work for a few years, then retire on time at sixty-five. I'd enjoy watching it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing at Northgate, keep learning the new kit as it comes, retire at sixty-five. Maybe I'd do a bit of part-time training for the supplier after that, if they wanted me. I'd tell Ines to start thinking about her café now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd find sad in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the end of the tea break. When there's nobody on site, there's no one to tell you a bad joke at ten o'clock. The work I can let go of, the people I'd miss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your retirement plans at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Sixty-five was always the plan, Paula's got a list of places she wants to go. If the supplier wanted me two days a week to teach, I'd think about it. But the reservoir and the drone are calling.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, so use it. Firms, government and ordinary people all have time to prepare.
S4.think: It barely touches me: I'd work with the early machines for a few years and retire on time at sixty-five. Honestly, I'd enjoy watching it happen.
S4.do: Keeps working at Northgate and learns new equipment as it arrives, retiring at sixty-five. May do part-time training for the robot supplier and urges his daughter to plan for her café.
S4.quote: The work I can let go of, the people I'd miss.
S4.fieldNote: He feels secure with a decade and is curious rather than worried. His loss would be social, not financial: the tea-break jokes. He would consider teaching after retirement.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, but not as much as people might think. It's the only one where I'd be rushing, and where Paula's job might go at the same time. What would help is a sensible way for older workers to retire a couple of years early if their trade goes, and firms paying for the training while they're making the savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask people whether they've actually worked next to one of these machines. Most people who are scared of it haven't. That doesn't mean they're wrong, but it's different once you've had to pull one out of a stairwell.

headlineQuote: It's different once you've had to pull one out of a stairwell.
portrait: Diego Baker is a 58-year-old fit-out carpenter at Northgate Construction who uses AI every day and is already the person who runs his site's layout robot. He'd find an AI plateau a bit dull and sees steady change as his chance to become the site's machine lead. Even the two-year AGI picture leaves him only uneasy, because his daily work with a robot convinces him the transition will need people like him for a few years. With five or ten years he is calm, even pleased, and plans to retire on time. His one real worry is his wife's job on school reception.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, as the only picture where he'd be rushing and his wife's job might go at the same time, though he worries less than most.
whatWouldHelp: A sensible way for older workers to retire a couple of years early if their trade goes, and firms paying for training while they make the savings.
